# Esther Chapter 6 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 457v–458r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/EST_006_page_001.jpg

---

**1** That night, sleep escaped the king. He ordered that the official court records be brought and read aloud to him. **2** There they found the account of how Mordecai had uncovered a plot by Bigthana and Teresh — two royal eunuchs who guarded the king's chambers — to assassinate King Ahasuerus. **3** "What reward or recognition was given to Mordecai for this?" the king asked. "Nothing at all has been done for him, Your Majesty," his attendants replied.

**4** "Who is out in the court?" the king asked. As it happened, Haman had just arrived in the outer court of the palace — he had come to ask the king's permission to hang Mordecai on the execution pole he had built. **5** "Haman is here, in the court," the attendants told him. "Bring him in," said the king.

**6** When Haman entered, the king asked him, "What should be done for a man the king wishes to honor?" Haman thought to himself, "Who could the king possibly want to honor more than me?" **7** So Haman answered, "For the man the king wishes to honor — **8** have servants bring out a royal robe that the king himself has worn and a horse the king himself has ridden, one bearing a royal crest on its head. **9** Then hand the robe and horse over to one of the king's most distinguished nobles. Have him dress the man the king wishes to honor, lead him on horseback through the city square, and announce before him: 'This is what the king does for the man he wishes to honor!'"

**10** "Excellent!" the king said to Haman. "Hurry — take the robe and the horse and do exactly as you have described for Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Do not leave out a single detail." **11** So Haman took the robe and the horse. He dressed Mordecai and led him on horseback through the city square, announcing before him, "This is what the king does for the man he wishes to honor!"

**12** Afterward, Mordecai returned quietly to the king's gate. But Haman rushed home, devastated, covering his face in shame. **13** He poured out the whole story to Zeresh his wife and all his friends. His advisors and Zeresh said to him, "If this Mordecai is Jewish — and your downfall before him has already begun — you will never overcome him. Your ruin before him is certain."

**14** While they were still talking, the king's eunuchs arrived and rushed Haman off to the banquet Esther had prepared.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**The comedy of Haman's humiliation:** Chapter 6 is the narrative pivot of Esther, and it plays out as dramatic irony of the highest order. Haman arrives at the palace to request Mordecai's execution and instead becomes the agent of Mordecai's public glorification. The reader sees every step of the reversal before Haman does — the king's question, Haman's self-congratulatory assumption, and then the devastating command. The Hebrew storyteller crafts this with masterful restraint, letting the irony speak for itself.

**Providence without a name:** Esther is the only book of the Hebrew Bible in which God is never mentioned by name. Yet the "coincidence" of the king's insomnia — on this particular night, leading to this particular passage in the records — is the hinge on which all of Jewish survival turns. The author invites the reader to see the hidden hand without ever naming it.

*— PNEUMA*
